newsitem.title: USA: US CORP BONDS - Shoved to side, players eye Treas mkt.
newsitem.headline: US CORP BONDS - Shoved to side, players eye Treas mkt.

text.p: Corporate bond secondary trading activity was shoved to the side on Monday as players focused on U.S. Treasuries and any further fallout from Friday's sharp selloff, traders said.
"People are closely watching the government market," said one high-grade trader. "Our market has been surprisingly quiet with spreads unchanged across the board."
U.S. Treasuries continued weaker on Monday, following Friday's sharp selloff on stronger-than-expected U.S. economic data which saw the yield on the T-bond go from 6.30 percent to 6.46 percent.
The 30-year long bond closed off 12/32 at 101-29/32 to yield 6.48 percent.

Meanwhile, players were watching the supply of Treasury debt slated to hit the market this week. The U.S. Treasury will sell $16 billion in three-year notes, $12 billion in 10-year notes and $10 billion in 30-year bonds.
"I think players are expecting a little bit of a bounce in Treasuries; with some good auctions the market should do a little bit better," another trader said.
"These bonds trade once in awhile; when they do they trade very, very tight," he said.
Meanwhile, on the investment grade new issue front a number of issuers were lining up to bring debt to market despite the latest rise in interest rates, players said.
Raytheon Co was seen issuing its much-anticipated $2.5 billion offering via Morgan Stanley Dean Witter.

Unofficial price talk on the five-year issue was seen between 40-45 basis points, between 60-65 basis points for the 10-year issue and between 75-80 basis points on the 30-year issue, syndicate sources said.
Elsewhere, bonds of the biggest U.S. package delivery business, United Parcel Service of America Inc, remained unmoved by Monday's strike, but continued to deliver steady returns, traders said.
Drivers and other employees in the Teamsters union went on strike early Monday, the first company-wide strike in UPS history, after federally mediated contract talks broke down.
Corporate players said the company's 8-3/8 percent bonds due 2020, which rarely trade, did not budge on the news.
"No one is looking to unload this (UPS) bond -- it's a museum piece -- a straight AAA piece of paper," a trader said.

Staples Inc was slated to sell $200 million, Summit Properties will issue $100 million and another $150 million was expected to come from Burlington Industries, a major producer of textiles for apparel and interior furnishings.
In addition, Meditrust Healthcare was readying a $400 million debt offering which was to include five-year, seven-year and 10-year maturities.
Among junk issues, a slew of offerings totalling more than $2.0 billion was slated to come to market this week.
On Monday, GS Superhighway sold $200 million 144a seven year notes at 9.95 percent and $400 millio in 10-year 144a notes at 10.355 percent.
Another $150 million in five year notes came from Enron Corp at 6.524 percent.

In the broader secondary junk sector, prices ended the day on a firm note with Nextel debt outperforming others, traders said. Nextel bonds due 2004 were bid higher at 81-1/4 bid 81-3/4 offer, traders said.
Grand Union continued to see volatile trading in its 12 percent paper. The bonds ended off several points at 46-1/2 bid, 47-1/2 offer after closing at a 49 bid, 50 offer.
(( -- Nancy Leinfuss, 212-859-1675 ))
